subject: Economics and Business
name: Economics and Business, Levels 9 and 10
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: Economics and Business, Levels 9 and 10

chapters.title: The circular flow of the economy

points.title: The two-sector circular flow model
points.brief: Households sell their labour and other resources to businesses for income, then spend that income on the goods and services businesses make, so money flows in a loop.

points.title: Adding government, finance and the overseas sector
points.brief: The five-sector model adds government, financial institutions and other countries, through taxes and spending, saving and investment, and imports and exports.

points.title: Leakages and injections
points.brief: Saving, tax and imports leak money out of the flow, while investment, government spending and exports inject it back. If injections exceed leakages, the economy grows.

points.title: How the sectors depend on each other
points.brief: Each sector relies on the others, so a fall in household spending cuts business sales, then jobs and incomes, then tax revenue.

points.title: Economic growth and GDP
points.brief: Gross domestic product is the value of all final goods and services made in a country in a year. Growth is the rise in real GDP, which removes the effect of price rises.

points.title: The unemployment rate
points.brief: The unemployment rate is the share of the labour force without a job who are looking for one. High unemployment wastes resources and lowers living standards.

points.title: Inflation and the CPI
points.brief: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, measured by the consumer price index, which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods and services.

points.title: The business cycle
points.brief: The economy moves through booms and slowdowns rather than growing evenly. Indicators such as GDP, jobs and inflation show which phase it is in.

points.title: How indicators guide decisions
points.brief: Governments, the Reserve Bank, businesses and households watch indicators to decide on policy, hiring, investment and spending.

points.title: Living standards
points.brief: Material living standards are the goods and services people can afford, often measured by GDP per person. Non-material ones include health, safety, the environment and free time.

points.title: Government's economic aims
points.brief: The government aims for strong, steady growth, low unemployment, stable prices and a fair share of income, to raise living standards.

points.title: The federal budget
points.brief: Each year the federal government sets out its planned revenue and spending. Spending more than it raises is a deficit; raising more than it spends is a surplus.

points.title: Expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy
points.brief: To lift a slow economy, government spends more or cuts taxes. To slow an overheating one and cool inflation, it spends less or raises taxes.

points.title: Other ways government intervenes
points.brief: Government also shapes the economy with welfare payments, regulations, subsidies and competition laws, to fix problems markets leave and protect consumers.

points.title: The Reserve Bank of Australia
points.brief: The RBA is Australia's central bank. Its Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy independently of the government, to keep prices stable and support full employment.

points.title: The cash rate
points.brief: The cash rate is the interest rate on overnight loans between banks, set by the RBA. Banks' rates on home loans and savings tend to follow it.

points.title: How interest rates affect spending
points.brief: Raising the cash rate makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so spending and inflation slow. Cutting it does the opposite.

points.title: The inflation target
points.brief: The RBA aims to keep inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average, because low, steady inflation helps people and businesses plan.

points.title: Why countries trade
points.brief: Countries trade because each is better at making some things than others. By specialising and trading, both sides can have more than if each made everything itself.

points.title: Australia's exports and imports
points.brief: Australia mostly exports minerals such as iron ore, coal and gas, farm products, education and tourism, and imports manufactured goods such as cars, phones and fuel.

points.title: Australia's changing trade partners
points.brief: Australia once traded mostly with the United Kingdom. Today most of its trade is with Asia, and China is its largest trading partner.

points.title: Globalisation
points.brief: Globalisation is the growing connection of the world's economies through trade, investment, money, technology and the movement of people.

points.title: Costs and benefits of globalisation
points.brief: Globalisation brings cheaper goods, bigger markets and new jobs, but can also cost some local jobs, widen inequality and spread economic shocks between countries.

points.title: Trade agreements and tariffs
points.brief: A tariff is a tax on imports that protects local producers but raises prices. Free trade agreements cut tariffs between countries to increase trade.

points.title: What competitive advantage is
points.brief: A competitive advantage is something that lets a business beat its rivals and win customers, such as lower prices, better quality or a unique product.

points.title: Cost leadership and differentiation
points.brief: A business can compete by having the lowest costs and prices, or by making its product different and better in ways customers will pay more for.

points.title: The marketing mix
points.brief: Marketing decisions cover the 4 Ps: the product, its price, the place it is sold and how it is promoted.

points.title: Branding and digital marketing
points.brief: A strong brand makes a business easy to recognise and trust. Social media, influencers and targeted online ads now carry much of a brand's message.

points.title: Public relations
points.brief: Public relations manages how the public sees a business, through media releases, sponsorships, community work and handling bad news well.

points.title: Keeping an advantage through entrepreneurship
points.brief: Rivals copy successful ideas, so businesses keep their edge by innovating, improving products and finding new markets.

points.title: Human resource management
points.brief: Human resource management is how a business finds, trains, rewards and looks after its staff, so they work well and the business competes better.

points.title: Recruiting and selecting staff
points.brief: Businesses advertise a job, sort applications, interview and check references to choose the person whose skills best fit the role.

points.title: Training and development
points.brief: Training builds the skills staff need now, while development prepares them for future roles. Both raise productivity and help keep good staff.

points.title: Motivating employees
points.brief: Staff can be motivated with money, such as pay rises and bonuses, and without it, such as recognition, flexible hours and chances to grow.

points.title: Productivity and competitiveness
points.brief: Well-managed, motivated staff produce more for each hour worked, which cuts costs and helps a business compete.

points.title: Pay and conditions
points.brief: Minimum pay and conditions are set by the National Employment Standards and awards. Enterprise agreements, bargained at a workplace, can add more.

points.title: The Fair Work system
points.brief: The Fair Work Commission sets minimum wages and awards and settles disputes. The Fair Work Ombudsman helps workers and employers and enforces the rules.

points.title: Trade unions
points.brief: A trade union is a group of workers who join together to bargain for better pay, conditions and safety, and to support members in disputes.

points.title: Employer groups
points.brief: Employer groups represent businesses, advising them on workplace law, bargaining with unions and speaking for business to government.

points.title: Risk and return
points.brief: Investments that can earn more usually carry more risk of losing money. Safer choices such as bank savings usually earn less.

points.title: Ways to invest
points.brief: People can invest in savings accounts and term deposits, shares, property, bonds or managed funds, each with its own mix of risk, return and how quickly it can be sold.

points.title: Diversification
points.brief: Spreading money across different investments means one loss does less harm. It is the idea behind not putting all your eggs in one basket.

points.title: Insurance
points.brief: Insurance pays a regular premium to protect against a large loss, such as a car crash, a house fire or illness. An excess is the part the insured pays first.

points.title: Investment scams
points.brief: Promises of high returns with no risk, pressure to act fast and unlicensed advisers are signs of an investment scam. ASIC's Moneysmart lists licensed businesses.

points.title: Legal and ethical investing
points.brief: Investors must follow the law, and many also choose ethical investments that avoid harm, such as funds that leave out tobacco or fossil fuels.

points.title: What superannuation is
points.brief: Superannuation is money saved during working life for retirement, held in a super fund and invested until the person retires.

points.title: Who contributes to super
points.brief: Employers must pay the Superannuation Guarantee, 12 per cent of ordinary pay, into an employee's fund. Workers can add their own voluntary contributions.

points.title: How super grows
points.brief: Super is invested for decades, so compound returns make it grow a lot. Fees and the choice of fund make a big difference to the final balance.

points.title: Super and living standards
points.brief: Super lets people live better in retirement, and it means fewer rely fully on the Age Pension, which eases pressure on the budget as the population ages.

points.title: Big financial decisions
points.brief: Choices such as buying a car, renting or buying a home, or taking out a loan depend on income, interest rates, total cost over time and personal goals.

points.title: Cost-benefit analysis
points.brief: Cost-benefit analysis lists and, where possible, values all the costs and benefits of an option. If benefits outweigh costs, the option is worth taking.

points.title: Evaluating with criteria
points.brief: Options can be compared against criteria chosen in advance, such as cost, fairness, effect on the environment and how quickly it works.

points.title: Validity of sources
points.brief: A valid source is authentic and accurate. Check who made it, their purpose and expertise, when it was made and whether other evidence supports it.

points.title: Predicting from trends
points.brief: Spotting trends and cause-and-effect links in data lets economists make logical predictions, such as rising rates slowing house prices.
